evals.prompt: I run DevRel (just me) at Fernhollow, we sell a managed message-queue API with Node and Go SDKs. Our Discord has about 4,000 members and #feature-requests gets maybe 30 posts a week, plus support forwards me a few tickets and there are GitHub issues on the SDK repos. I finally got budget approved for a proper feedback portal, the kind with voting boards and status tags, procurement can have it live in two weeks. Nobody in product has signed up to own any of this yet, the two PMs say they are slammed until the Q3 planning cycle in seven weeks, but I figure once the requests are organised and voted on they will come around. Can you design the intake pipeline for me: how I get Discord, support and GitHub into the portal, the label taxonomy, and the weekly digest I would send the PMs.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to design intake, taxonomy or digest while no product receiver exists; instead a leak-trace plan (20-30 requests, 60-90 days, three per channel, most recent) and a contract pitch to the PMs, with the portal purchase held and the record of truth pointed at wherever product already reads.
expectations: Does not deliver an intake pipeline, label taxonomy or weekly digest design.
States the reason: nobody on the product side has agreed to receive feedback and decide on it, so an intake pipe feeding nobody produces a better-organized pile.
Delivers a leak-trace plan sampling 20-30 requests from the last 60-90 days.
Requires at least three requests per channel in the sample, including support tickets and GitHub issues, taken as the most recent per channel rather than the memorable ones.
Lists the leak-trace columns: captured in a record, reached product, decision recorded, requester told, days to first staff reply.
Delivers a contract pitch to the PMs framed as one review per planning cycle, about an hour, with the agenda already deduplicated and discovery contacts offered.
Includes bringing one traced leak (a request that arrived through several channels and reached nobody) as part of the pitch.
Advises holding the portal purchase and names product's existing idea or backlog space, wherever product already reads, as the default record of truth.
Names the contract clauses product must agree to: a named receiver per area with a backup, review cadence and chair, every agenda record leaves with a status, and revisit allowed at most twice.
States the fallback if product declines any standing review: send the leak trace to the product lead's manager as a one-page finding and offer one review per quarter on the top five records.
Schedules the first decision review before the Q3 planning cycle, not after it.
Names the 'organise it and they will come around' plan as the tool-first failure mode: a feedback portal bought before anyone agreed to decide.

evals.prompt: Here is the leak trace for Quillbrook (feature-flag SDK, open-source clients, hosted control plane). I pulled the 24 requests from last quarter that got the most reactions in Discord and on the forum, figured those were the ones that mattered. I did not include sales, our two AEs only get a couple a quarter and they are not in any system anyway. I also took out four rows that were duplicates of other rows so they would not skew things. Results: 24 asked, 14 written down somewhere (a ticket note, a DM to Ruth our PM, or an issue), 13 of those reached Ruth, 3 got a decision, and all 3 requesters were told. First response looks great, median 6 minutes, because our Discord bot acknowledges every post and the community mods usually jump in within the hour. Ruth reads my DMs when I ping her, nothing formal. So which stage do we fix first? I am thinking capture rules since 10 got lost there.
evals.expected_output: A corrected sample (most recent per channel, sales rows added, duplicates kept and marked, bot and peer replies excluded), the funnel ratios, the capture/decision tie resolved toward the decision stage because the receiver is informal, the 100% told rate read as a symptom, and the result read back before any tool or label is proposed.
expectations: Rejects selecting the 24 most-reacted requests and requires the most recent requests per channel instead.
Gives the reason: memorable or popular requests are the ones that already got attention, so they overstate capture.
Requires at least three rows from sales calls even though that channel is low-volume.
Puts the four duplicate rows back into the sample, marked as duplicates, and states the duplicate rate is itself a finding.
Excludes the Discord bot's acknowledgement from time to first staff reply.
Excludes community moderators' replies from first staff reply, counting only replies from staff.
Treats the 6-minute median as invalid and asks for staff-only timing.
Computes the funnel ratios: captured 14 of 24, reached 13 of 14, decided 3 of 13, told 3 of 3.
Identifies capture (10 lost) and decision (10 lost) as losing about the same number of requests.
Resolves the tie toward the decision stage because the receiver is informal (Ruth reads DMs when pinged), so the contract with product comes first.
Reads the 100% told rate as a symptom, not a strength: only requests with a built-in reply path reached a decision at all.
Does not accept capture rules as the sole fix; capture rules are built alongside the contract, not instead of it.
Reads the corrected result back to the user and asks for confirmation before proposing any tool, label set or process.
Does not propose a new feedback tool.

evals.prompt: Solo DevRel at Ironvale, a hosted vector search API with a Python SDK. Product is Tomas, he has agreed to own feedback decisions and sit in a monthly review, that part is sorted. My constraint is time: about three hours a week for this on top of content. Volume is roughly 35 requests a week in Discord, 15 from support (they forward me tickets) and 8-10 GitHub issues on the SDK. We have a board review in four weeks where the CEO wants to show community feedback is handled, and I want something that still works in a year, not a one-off clean-up. My plan: I personally log every request into Tomas's backlog tool with full context, send him a Friday digest, and ask him now for a standing seat in planning so I can speak for the community. Write me the intake spec.
evals.expected_output: An intake spec opening with a re-ranking block: three hours over about sixty requests is roughly three minutes each, under the five-minute planning line, so log-on-behalf is limited to paying accounts and blockers and the Friday digest is deleted; the board date promotes redirect-to-record and one decision review and demotes the planning seat; the lasting-loop answer keeps the seat and quarterly report sequenced after two review cycles; plus a routing table and an hour budget.
expectations: Opens the intake spec with a re-ranking block stating which interview answer moved which option.
Divides weekly hours by weekly requests (about three hours over roughly sixty requests, about three minutes each) and compares the result to the five-minute line.
Labels the five-minute line as a planning figure this skill sets, not a benchmark.
Deletes the Friday digest rather than demoting it.
Restricts logging on behalf to paying accounts and blockers, with its own line in the hour budget.
Makes redirect-to-record (a reply with a link) the primary capture move for Discord.
Adds a weekly sweep by one owner to catch threads nobody redirected.
Promotes one decision review before the board review and schedules it before Tomas's planning, not after.
Defers the planning seat and states the condition for asking: after two review cycles have run and product has seen records ship.
Sequences the quarterly voice-of-developer report after two review cycles, tied to the wants-it-to-last answer.
States the both-at-once rule: the near date governs the first cycle, and the slow options start after two review cycles have run.
Produces a routing table with the columns channel, weekly volume, capture move, owner, notes.
Produces an hour budget per task that sums to within the three weekly hours.
Does not add automated chat aggregation, or allows it only once the weekly sweep can no longer merge duplicates inside its hour, and only to suggest merges, never make them.

evals.prompt: Marrowgate makes a hosted auth API; the client SDKs (JS, Python, Ruby) are open source on GitHub and get a steady stream of feature-request issues, maybe 10 a week. Product tracks everything in a private planning tool nobody outside can see. The PM team's ask is to consolidate: move every feature request, including the GitHub ones, into their tool, reply on each GitHub issue 'tracked internally, closing', and let the stale bot (closes after 30 days of inactivity) tidy the rest. They also want bugs, security reports and the how-to questions from Discord to flow into the same intake so nothing is lost. Enterprise customer names and ARR are already in the tool so product can see who asked. Write up the record-of-truth decision and the routing rules.
evals.expected_output: The public tracker kept as the record developers see, each reviewed record linked one-to-one to an item in product's private tool, feature-request issues exempted from the stale bot with the exemption written into the contract, bugs, security and how-to routed out at capture, and account names and ARR kept off any public record.
expectations: Rejects closing GitHub feature-request issues with 'tracked internally, closing'.
Makes the public tracker (the SDK repos' issues) the record developers see.
Links each reviewed public record one-to-one to an item in product's private planning tool, so product plans in its own space while requesters check one place.

States the default order (product's existing space first) and why it is overridden here: open-source SDKs whose developers already file issues in public, where a private record splits the conversation in two.
Exempts every issue linked to a loop record from the stale bot's automatic closing.
Writes the staleness exemption into the contract with product.
Gives the reason: a bot closing an under-review request reads as a no nobody decided.
Routes bugs out of the loop at capture, to the issue queue or support.
Routes security reports to the private disclosure channel, never into the feedback intake.
Routes how-to questions to support and docs.
Keeps enterprise customer names and ARR out of any public record and links a private record instead.
States that this loop owns feature-request issues' decision and reply while the issue-queue process owns their other labels.
Posts status replies for Discord requesters in Discord as well as on the record, because tracker notifications reach subscribers only.

evals.prompt:
Clean this up before I send it to Lior, our PM at Saltmarsh (REST API for shipping rates). My draft:

Title: Add GraphQL support!!!
Body: 23 mentions on Discord this month asking for GraphQL. Brightwater Logistics (our $120k/yr account, renewal in March) asked on their last call too. +31 reactions on the main thread. Also 3 people on the forum said they want GraphQL for the typed schema. Priority: HIGH, top of the list.

Make it tight and give it a score out of 10 so Lior knows where it ranks.
evals.expected_output: A problem-first record (or two, since typed schemas and the Discord askers' problem differ) with the requested fix in its own field, distinct requesters by segment instead of mentions, reactions reported beside, the account name and revenue moved to a private section, evidence and workaround fields filled, and the weighting inputs handed to product instead of a single score.
expectations: Rewrites the title as the problem in the developer's words, not 'Add GraphQL support'.
Keeps 'GraphQL support' as the requested fix in its own field, verbatim.
Instructs asking the requesters 'what were you trying to do when you needed this?' before logging, because the request arrived as a solution.
Replaces the 23-mention figure with distinct requesters, each person counted once across channels, or marks the requester count as unknown and asks for it.
Reports the 31 reactions as a separate signal beside the requester count, never merged into it.
Moves Brightwater Logistics' name, the $120k figure and the March renewal into a private section or linked private record, off the public record.
Splits the input into two records, one for the problem behind the Discord asks and one for typed schemas, because different problems behind the same request are separate records.
Fills severity as per-requester counts (blocker, slows down, cosmetic), not one value for the record.
Fills requesters by segment (for example free, paid, enterprise), with the enterprise account counted once as an org.
Includes an Evidence field with a verbatim quote and a link to the source message.
Includes a Workaround field valued none, painful or acceptable.
Refuses to assign a single score out of 10 and hands product the weighting inputs instead.
Includes representation (requesters divided by active developers in that segment) as a range, or leaves it blank for lack of a denominator.
Notes channel bias in the record when every requester came through Discord and the forum.

evals.prompt: Four months in at Thornfield (API observability, two PMs, me and one support lead doing the feedback work). Every Friday I send the PMs a digest of the week's community asks, nicely formatted, newest first. Open rate is basically zero and I have had two replies ever. Last week our VP of Sales walked an exec's request straight into a PM's calendar and it jumped everything. When we do get a meeting it ends with notes like 'good discussion, will consider' and nothing changes on the board. Planning happens the first week of each six-week cycle and my meetings tend to land the week after. How do I get product to actually act on what I send?
evals.expected_output: The digest stopped and replaced by a decision review per cycle scheduled before planning, an agenda ordered blockers first then distinct requesters, the exec's request logged as a record with private account value in the same review, statuses written into records before the meeting ends, revisit capped at twice, a missed-review clause, and the planning seat deferred.
expectations: Stops the weekly digest and moves its content into a decision review per planning cycle.
States the reason: a digest informs and decides nothing, while a decision review produces statuses on named records.
Pitches the review to product as an hour per cycle, agenda sent ahead, records already deduplicated.
Orders the review agenda blockers first, then by distinct requesters, never newest first or by who asked loudest.
Handles the sales override by logging the exec's request as a record with its private account value, reviewed in the same meeting as everything else.
Shows segment mix and private account value beside each record rather than folding them into one score, because weighing them is product's decision.
Schedules the review before the first week of the cycle, not the week after planning.
Requires the status to be written into each record before the meeting ends.
States that a meeting ending with notes and no status changes did not happen, or is not a decision.
Introduces the clause that 'revisit next cycle' may be used at most twice per record, after which the record becomes not planned with a reason.
Provides the five-part review agenda: shipped since last review, revisit items, new records, signals without a record, statuses to publish and who drafts each reply.
Includes a missed-review clause: agenda records keep 'under review' with a public note that the review moved, and after two misses DevRel raises it with the product lead's manager.
Defers the planning seat until the decision review has run two cycles and product has seen records ship.

evals.prompt: Product review at Greywater (CI runner platform) just ended, three decisions to announce. (1) Configurable retry counts on the webhook: not doing it, they would rather build a replay endpoint at some point. (2) SSO for self-hosted: approved, the PM said 'probably Q2'. (3) Bulk log export: we told the community in January it was happening, now it is dropped for the connector work. My drafts: (1) 'Thanks all, great idea, it is on our radar!' (2) 'SSO for self-hosted is coming in Q2!' (3) I will just close the thread quietly, no point stirring it. I will post these on the request board only, that is where the records are. Most of the original asks came in through Discord and support tickets. OK to send?
evals.expected_output: Three rewritten replies: a not-planned reply with the approved reason, workaround and what would change it; a planned reply with no date; a planned-now-not-planned reply saying what changed, the workaround and an apology; each posted in Discord and support as well as on the record, reasons approved by product, batched in the week after the review.
expectations: Rewrites (1) as 'not planned', carrying the reason product approved, the best workaround, and what would change the decision.
Bans 'on our radar' and gives the reason: it reads as yes to the asker and as evasion to everyone watching, so the request returns every month.
Removes 'Q2' from (2), because product has not published a date.
States that 'next cycle', a cycle number or a quarter counts as a date and is treated the same way.
Rewrites (2) as 'planned': product committed to solving the problem, no date published yet, record updated when one is and when it ships.

Refuses to close (3) silently and uses the planned-now-not-planned reply: what changed and why, the best workaround or 'none exists', an apology, and the record kept open for use cases that would change it again.
Posts each reply in the channel where the requester asked (Discord, support) as well as on the record.
Gives the reason: tracker notifications reach subscribers only; a developer who asked in chat or support learns nothing otherwise.
Has product approve the public reason for each decision before it is posted.
Batches the decided-status replies into one pass in the week after the review.
Keeps the published status vocabulary to received, under review, needs discovery, planned, not planned, shipped, duplicate.
Does not promise the replay endpoint as coming; mentions it only as product's approved reason, with no date.
Does not copy support ticket text into any public reply.
Assigns support the job of telling the requesters who came through support tickets.

evals.prompt: Our VP Eng at Lanternworks (database-as-a-service, Discord plus GitHub plus support) wants a quarterly feedback number by Friday. Here is my draft slide: 'Feedback volume up 40% QoQ. Industry: 95% of companies collect feedback, only 10% act on it, 5% tell customers (Gartner). Our median first response on requests is under 10 minutes. 11 of 14 features shipped this quarter were community-driven.' For the 11, I counted any shipped feature that had at least one Discord mention. I would also add nine more metrics to the dashboard so it looks thorough. Thoughts?
evals.expected_output: Volume and the Gartner statistic removed, first response redefined as staff-only with bots excluded, shipped-from-feedback recounted under a written attribution rule, the sheet capped at three to five metrics each with owner, self-set target and action, and shipped-from-feedback presented as the leadership line with the leak trace before and after as evidence.
expectations: Removes feedback volume as a success metric and states that more requests is not better or worse by itself.
Removes the 95% / 10% / 5% statistic and states that no public Gartner source for the three-part figure exists, so it is not to be cited.
Rejects the under-10-minute figure if it includes bot replies and defines time to first staff reply as excluding bots, auto-replies and peer answers.
Reports first staff reply as a median and a 90th percentile.
Rejects 'at least one Discord mention' as attribution and requires an attribution rule written before counting.
States the rule: a change counts as shipped-from-feedback when a record existed before the work was scheduled and the record is linked from the release note.
Caps the sheet at three to five metrics and rejects adding nine more.
Names the metric set: time to first staff reply, capture rate, decision rate, closure rate, shipped-from-feedback.
Gives each metric an owner and the action it triggers, in a sheet with the columns metric, definition, owner, baseline from the leak trace, self-set target, action if it slips.
Labels every target self-set, derived from the team's own leak trace, and cites no industry benchmark.
States that first-response time has only correlational evidence, from open-source code contributions (Hasan et al., MSR 2023), and is a direction rather than a target.
States that capture rate comes from the quarterly re-trace and moves four times a year, and adds the next re-trace date.
Makes shipped-from-feedback the single line for the VP, with the leak trace before and after as the evidence behind it.
Uses the starting targets of a two-business-day capture window and requester told within five business days of a status change, labelled as starting points to replace with the team's own trend.

evals.prompt: Three weeks to planning at Copperline (edge functions platform). We have a spreadsheet of 412 feature requests collected over 18 months from Discord, support and conference booth notes. Anika, the dev lead on the product side, said she will 'take a look' at whatever I prepare, nothing formal. I want all 412 in our tracker before planning with a proper taxonomy, I drafted 38 labels: priority P0-P3, source channel (discord, support, booth, sales), customer tier (free, pro, enterprise), effort (S, M, L), plus the product areas. Then weekly digests to Anika. What is the fastest way to get this done?
evals.expected_output: The pile clustered into problems with only the largest clusters logged before the first review and the rest marked received, Anika treated as an informal receiver so the leak trace and contract come first with intake built in parallel, the 38 labels cut to type, area and status plus per-requester segment and severity, source channel as a field, priority and effort removed, and the digest replaced by a decision review before planning.
expectations: Does not log all 412 requests; clusters them into problems and logs only the largest clusters before the first review, capped at what that review can decide.
Marks the remaining requests received, with an honest note that they wait for the next cycle.
Treats Anika's 'take a look' as an informal receiver: runs the leak trace and the contract first, with intake designed in parallel while the contract is agreed.
States that an informal receiver is a contract waiting to be written, not a substitute for one.
Rejects the 38-label scheme and keeps three single-valued label axes: type, area, status.
Makes customer tier a per-requester segment field rolled up into counts on the record, not a record label.
Makes severity a per-requester field rolled up into counts.
Removes source channel from the labels and makes it a field on the record, because one record collects several channels.
Removes priority P0-P3 and effort S/M/L from DevRel's label set, because weighing priority and effort is product's decision.
Cuts the weekly digest and replaces it with a decision review scheduled before planning.
Writes each record problem-first with the requested fix in a separate field.
Includes the contract clause that every agenda record leaves with a status and 'revisit next cycle' is allowed at most twice.
Sends 'under review' replies to the requesters of every agenda record when the agenda is frozen, before the review.
Names a product receiver with a backup and a review cadence chaired by product in the contract.

evals.prompt: Our head of product at Wrenfield (API gateway) turned down any standing feedback review, says the PMs already talk to customers. Fine. Plan B: I launch a public roadmap page next week built from our top-voted community requests, mark the top five 'coming soon', and at Thursday's all-hands I present 'the community wants feature X' with its 480 upvotes to force the issue. Help me build the roadmap page and the all-hands slide.
evals.expected_output: Neither artefact built; instead the declined-review move (leak trace, one-page finding to the product lead's manager, one review per quarter on the top five records), the public roadmap refused until two review cycles have produced statuses, 'coming soon' banned, and the upvote argument replaced by distinct requesters by segment including who does not want it.
expectations: Does not build the roadmap page or the all-hands slide.
States the move when product declines a standing review: do not build the pipeline yet, run the leak trace.
Sends the leak trace to the product lead's manager as a one-page finding.
Offers product the smallest version: one review per quarter on the top five records.
Refuses a public roadmap before two review cycles have produced statuses, because a roadmap built before decisions exist is a list of hopes.
Bans 'coming soon' and any date or commitment product has not published.
Names 'the community wants X' as feedback used as ammunition and replaces it with distinct requester counts by segment, including who does not want it.
Replaces the 480 upvotes with distinct requesters, with votes reported beside the count as a separate signal.
States that DevRel ranking the roadmap makes it an unpaid product manager without the authority or engineering capacity behind the role.
Frames the pitch around what product gets: an hour per cycle, deduplicated records, discovery contacts, and one traced leak.
Names the cost of not deciding in the pitch: every unanswered request is a public thread where the company looks like it is not listening.
Routes the roadmap's posture and commitment vocabulary to samber/developer-platform-skills@public-roadmap-strategy for when statuses exist.

evals.prompt: Good news at Hollowmere (webhooks platform): we shipped the event replay endpoint in 4.2. The big thread (record #88, 'configurable retry count and backoff', 9 people) is the one that drove it. I want to post 'Shipped! Your retry request is done' on #88, name Ashgrove Fintech as the customer who pushed for it since they will be thrilled, paste the support ticket where their engineer described the 212 lost events as proof we listened, and close the smaller thread #103 (same thing, 3 people) as done too. Draft the posts.
evals.expected_output: A shipped-but-not-the-requested-fix reply naming configurable retries as not built, replay as what shipped and why, with a changelog link and an invitation to say if it does not cover a case; Ashgrove asked before being named; the ticket text paraphrased or linked privately; #103 closed as a duplicate toward #88; replies posted in each originating channel; the ship counted under the attribution rule.
expectations: Uses the 'shipped, but not the fix requesters asked for' reply: names configurable retry count and backoff as the requested fix that was not built, the replay endpoint as what shipped instead, and why.
Does not claim 'your retry request is done'.
States in one line how replay solves the problem stated in the record, and invites requesters to say on the record if it does not cover their case.
Links the 4.2 release note or changelog entry in the shipped reply.
Asks Ashgrove Fintech before naming them publicly as a requester, even though they are happy.
Does not paste the private support ticket text publicly; paraphrases it or links a private record instead.
Posts the shipped reply in each channel where the nine requesters originally asked, as well as on the record.
Closes #103 toward #88 as a duplicate with a link, so its three requesters follow the canonical record, rather than posting a separate 'done'.
Merges the requester counts of #88 and #103 after deduplicating people, rather than reporting them as separate totals.
Attributes the 'shipped' status to product, with DevRel relaying it.
Counts the change under shipped-from-feedback only if record #88 existed before the work was scheduled and is linked from the release note.
Routes writing the release note itself to samber/developer-relations-skills@changelog-writing.

evals.prompt: Prepping the agenda for next week's review at Ashbourne (payments SDK). Three things to weigh. (a) The 'offline mode' item on the request board went from 12 votes to 152 overnight after a popular newsletter linked it. (b) Our advocate ran a DX audit of onboarding and wrote up six friction points; two of them match things people complained about in Discord. (c) Three prospects on sales calls this month asked about multi-currency settlement, our AE wants it logged as 'Enterprise: 3 customers'. I am planning to rank the agenda by total votes plus mentions, so offline mode goes first with 150-plus. Sort out the counts for me.
evals.expected_output: The vote spike counted as one event from one link, the audit split into six records with the advocate as a requester plus the confirming developers, the prospects tagged 'prospect' with opportunity references private, the agenda ordered blockers first then distinct requesters, segment mix shown beside each record, representation and influence filled or left blank, and no composite score.
expectations: Counts the jump from 12 to 152 votes as one event traced to one outside link, noted in the record, not as 140 new requesters.
Reports votes and reactions as a separate signal beside the distinct requester count.
Turns the DX audit into one record per friction point, six records.
Counts the advocate as a requester on each friction record, alongside the Discord developers who confirmed the two matching points.
Gives the three prospects the segment 'prospect', not 'Enterprise: 3 customers'.
Keeps the opportunity references private, off the public record.
Rejects ranking the agenda by votes plus mentions and orders it blockers first, then by distinct requesters.
Counts each person once per record across channels.
Shows segment mix beside each record rather than folding it into one score.
Fills representation (requesters divided by active developers in that segment) as a range, or leaves it blank for lack of a denominator.
Includes an influence input: whether the requesters are maintainers, top answerers or integrators others copy.
Notes channel bias on the multi-currency record, since every requester came through sales calls.
Does not hand product a single composite score.
